item.title: GitHub Makes Agentic Workflows Generally Available with Isolation and Budget Controls
item.description:
GitHub Agentic Workflows is generally available, running coding agents in GitHub Actions with read-only defaults and separately scoped write jobs. Those protections do not cover direct write permissions or custom jobs, so they depend on how each workflow is configured.

By Mark Silvester

item.title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
item.description:
JioHotstar evaluated 6 approaches to code retrieval for AI coding agents using SWE, CodeScale Bench, and an internal question-answering harness. Structural search performed well on concrete tasks, while semantic retrieval helped with ambiguous requirements. The findings highlight trade-offs in accuracy, token use, and tool design, underscoring the need to match retrieval tools to task types.

By Leela Kumili

item.title: How LinkedIn, Netflix & DoorDash Run Agents, Evals & Inference in Production: QCon AI New York 2026
item.description:
QCon AI New York has published its full program for December 15–16, 2026. item.description:
Movers & Shakers is where you can keep up with new CIO appointments and gain valuable insight into the job market and CIO hiring trends. As every company becomes a technology company, CEOs and corporate boards are seeking multi-dimensional CIOs and IT leaders with superior skills in technology, communications, business strategy, and digital innovation. The role is more challenging than ever before — but even more exciting and rewarding! If you have CIO job news to share, please contact me here!

Publix

Founded in 1930, Publix Super Markets is an employee-owned supermarket chain in the US employing over 200,000 associates. Douglas currently serves as SVP and CIO, and has been with the company for more than 20 years. Before joining Publix, she served as SVP and CIO at FedEx. Douglas holds a BA from Duke University.

ABC Supply

ABC Supply distributes roofing materials, exterior and interior building products, and outdoor products to professional contractors. Sullivan, currently VP of software, data and digital transformation at the company, has led several key initiatives across AI, data and analytics, digital transformation and technology strategy. He held roles at Motorola Solutions and USG.

Alaska Airlines

Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, and Horizon Air are subsidiaries of Alaska Air Group, and McGee Air Services is a subsidiary of Alaska Airlines. It’s a global airline group with hubs in Seattle, Honolulu, Portland, Anchorage, Los Angeles, San Diego, and San Francisco. Siva was most recently chief digital and technology officer for health care delivery at CVS Health, where he led large-scale modernization and AI initiatives. He also held senior tech leadership roles at Target Corporation, where he helped rebuild Target.com and the Target app, and modernize infrastructure and cloud platforms. Siva holds a BTech from the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, and an MBA from XLRI Xavier School of Management.

Veralto

Veralto Corporation provides water analytics, water treatment, marking and coding, and packaging and color solutions worldwide. Jackson

Jackson National Life Insurance Company is the principal operating subsidiary of Jackson Financial Inc. Avantor

item.title: Taking AI-based transformations to the next level with prompt markup languages
item.description:
For engineers, one of generative AI’s chief selling points is its ability to write code using natural language. It may seem surprising, then, to learn that getting the most out of generative AI increasingly requires them to write code.

Specifically, engineers can benefit from what’s known as prompt markup languages, which provide the ability to control AI model behavior with greater precision, a key advantage for teams tasked with leveraging AI in contexts where reliability, accuracy and quality are vital.

Read on for details on how organizations can benefit from prompt markup languages, including my own business’s experience using this technique to help accelerate enterprise transformation projects.

The what and why of prompt markup languages

A prompt markup language is a programming language designed to structure and manage prompts that users feed into AI models.

For example, engineers could use a prompt markup language to define the specific role and tools that an AI model or agent can use when completing a task, or point it to the data sources it should leverage.

It’s possible, in theory, to give AI systems instructions in natural language that achieve these same ends. The problem with natural language, however, is that it’s ambiguous, and there’s no guarantee that models will interpret natural language prompts in the precise way the user expects. Nor is it possible to ensure that the same input will always yield the same output.

Prompt markup solves these challenges by allowing engineers to take a programmatic approach to feeding instructions into AI models. They can still use natural language to formulate parts of their prompts, but they can rely on markup to define key aspects. By extension, they can elicit more predictable, deterministic behavior from AI systems.

The benefits of prompt markup languages

To put this in more concrete terms, prompt markup languages deliver benefits like the following:

  • Component reusability: Markup makes it possible to build modular prompt components that can be reused across different AI workflows and applications.
  • Prompt chaining: Engineers can pass the output from one prompt directly into another to create multi-step AI workflows.
  • Prompt template support: With markup, teams can create reusable templates and change variables for different deliverables. This is much more efficient than writing a separate prompt for each one.
  • Tool control: Markup makes it possible to specify exactly which tools an AI model should use and under what circumstances. This mitigates the risk of having the model use the wrong tools. It can also help to streamline costs by requiring AI systems to use the most cost-effective tooling.
  • Conditionals and loops: Markup allows engineers to define structured logic, such as if-then conditions and repeatable loops, that the AI should follow consistently.

Prompt markup in the real world: Examples from the enterprise transformation space

By taking advantage of benefits like these, my organization (which specializes in helping clients transform and modernize enterprise software systems, such as SAP) has significantly accelerated transformation projects.

Many of our clients were already using AI to some degree to help with transformation. For instance, they were leveraging chatbots to help modernize legacy system code.

The problem they faced, however, was that complex enterprise software environments leave little room for error, and the open-ended nature of chatbots controlled using natural language didn’t always yield the necessary level of precision. Teams often had to iterate across multiple variations of prompts to get the results they sought, and even then, they weren’t always perfect.

To address this challenge, we built our own prompt markup language tailored for enterprise transformation. With a focus on capabilities like ontology awareness, audit-friendly evidence generation and repeatable workflows, the language has allowed us to leverage AI as an accelerator for transformation projects with a much higher degree of accuracy and predictability. It also saves a lot of time, thanks to the ability to leverage templates and prompt changes as a way of automating transformation tasks at scale.

Practical approaches to leveraging prompt markup

Admittedly, prompt markup languages are not without their challenges.

One is the need to generate prompt markup code, which generally takes longer than asking a natural language question, and typically requires an ‘engineering mindset’ to properly construct. It’s not for everyone in the enterprise.

Secondly, it’s critical for engineers to review and test markup code. While this might seem like extra work, it is very useful to prove to reviewers (such as auditors) that the right level of results is being generated.

However, without this type of approach, enterprises will constantly feel that AI is great, but not ready for the consistent, high-quality output they demand at scale. By addressing this challenge, prompt markup languages are poised to become a critical capability for all enterprises, especially those dealing with the complexities of large-scale IT-centric transformations.

item.title: As employees build AI agents, CIOs manage the lifecycle
item.description:
At Fujifilm Biotechnologies, an AI agent designed to help the legal department read contracts is gearing up to graduate from sandbox to full production in early December.

Contracts are a large part of the business at the CDMO, which partners with pharmaceutical and biotech companies to develop vaccines and therapies. The company’s legal team devised an agent to review contracts, check standards around terms and conditions, and propose edits for the legal team’s review.

“That’s a perfect use for a set of agents,” says Fujifilm Biotechnologies CDIO Mike Tomasco.

Similar types of AI agents that help enterprises and employees tackle time-consuming or repetitive work are cropping up in vast numbers across organizations. Gartner anticipates that by 2028, Fortune 500 companies will have on average more than 150,000 agents. Microsoft alone has deployed more than 500,000 internal agents, and HR, payroll, and workforce management platform UKG now has more agents than employees, according to its chief transformation officer, Prakash Kota.

As enterprise tools have made it easier for employees to spin up agents, CIOs are tasked with managing the lifecycles of agentic tools, advancing them from development to production, continuously measuring them against KPIs, and sunsetting them if they’re no longer meeting an organization’s needs.

As a result, IT leaders are thinking and talking differently about agents, says Madhu Narasimhan, CIO of healthcare organization DaVita.

“The conversation among CIOs has shifted from how do we build agents to how do we make sure they continue delivering value,” she says. “Getting an agent into production is no longer the hard part.”

Bringing agents to life

Managing the lifecycle of an AI agent starts before the build. CIOs and their teams outline the foundation and guardrails for employees to build, which then allows CIOs to govern agents through their lifespan and, if needed, eventually retire them.

Kevin McDonald, principal consultant at tech consulting firm Hylaine, advises leaders to define the job of an agent and build it with narrow permissions. “Treat an agent like a product with an owner, not a project with an end date,” he says.

Kota adds it’s important to balance IT visibility with employee autonomy, and recommends a playground where employees can experiment. He also recommends tech leaders assign dedicated identities to agents that are separate from user credentials and with a narrower scope of access.

At Fujifilm Biotechnologies, Tomasco wanted to take a deliberate approach to agentic AI, given the company’s position in a highly regulated industry. He didn’t want unfettered access to Claude Code like some companies have allowed.

That led him and his team to build an isolated sandbox called Genki Studio to encourage employees to experiment with agents without building them in the Wild West.

It’s a bring your own data environment with enterprise security controls, restricted network access, role-based permissions, and auditing, Tomasco says. All of the company’s 5,000 employees are eligible to apply to be part of the studio, though only a small portion have an interest and skillset in developing AI solutions. Fujifilm Biotechnologies prioritizes applicants with a relevant use case, strong interest in AI, and experience or familiarity with data and analytics. 

About 50 employees currently work in the studio, where they build prototypes of agents using leading AI models and the same tools developers have. Following the build, an employee invites coworkers to test the agents. Then, there’s typically a domain-based review to ensure the agent follows regulations and doesn’t duplicate something that already exists or is on the roadmap.

If all those factors line up, the agent can be released into production. The timeline from idea to release is typically six to eight weeks, according to Tomasco.

Measuring agent success and value

Once an agent is up and running, Fujifilm Biotechnologies assesses its utility over the next several weeks to determine if the agent should stay in production. It uses metrics such as adoption and KPIs specifically related to manufacturing processes, such as faster time to market for a pharmaceutical treatment.

The organization also checks on agents throughout their lifecycle to ensure they’re still fulfilling the originally designated purpose. “Agents can drift from the guardrails that you set up for them,” Tomasco says.

Meanwhile at DaVita, each agent goes through an internal AI intake and evaluation standard, Narasimhan says. The company spent over a year building a security and governance foundation before launching a company-wide AI platform this spring. To date, employees have created more than 10,000 agents, including ones that navigate questions on benefits or regulations, says Narasimhan.

“We assess compliance, cybersecurity, governance and business value before broader adoption,” she says. A team that includes staff from clinical, legal, cybersecurity and more will review each AI use case. KPIs for successful agents include accuracy, reliability, adoption, and business impact. If the agent is redundant or lacks engagement, DaVita considers decommissioning it. “I don’t believe in technology for technology’s sake,” she says.

Hylaine’s McDonald adds CIOs can assess agents on time savings, cost per task, and how frequently a human overrides an agent’s output. When override rates start to climb, or if running the agent costs more than the work it’s replacing, it may be time to sunset the agent, he says.

He recommends organizations maintain a registry of every agent with its permissions, versioned prompts, and tools. That way, when it’s time for agents to retire, CIOs can fully revoke access and prior context.

“Forgotten agents with live credentials are a real risk,” McDonald says.

Tomasco agrees that you have to be willing to just shut it down if an agent doesn’t hit established metrics. “There’s no sense in having something run that’s not creating value.”

The business, front and center

The topic of value, and whether AI agents deliver it, is increasingly top of mind for CIOs. Instead of measuring success by adoption or how many employees are building or using an AI agent, Kota says the focus now is how to convert that into business outcomes.

Employees spending their days experimenting in sandboxes or trialing agents doesn’t automatically translate to increased productivity or results for the organization as a whole, he says. “If we don’t impact the top line or reduce the bottom line impacts, what’s the purpose?”

For organizations like DaVita and Fujifilm Biotechnologies operating in high-stakes industries, use of AI agents speaks to a broader purpose to boost efficiencies that can save time for biopharma customers and patients.

“It’s exciting to be a part of it when you can help bring medicine to market faster for people,” Tomasco says. “It can be life-changing.”

item.title: The AI prototype worked. Who promised the launch?
item.description:
“Sure, we can figure it out.”

Earlier in my career, I used those words to avoid an uncomfortable conversation. I meant I would assess the request and explore what was possible. The person asking could hear that I had accepted the work and would deliver what they wanted.

I learned to be explicit, sometimes to the point of repeating myself. What felt redundant to me helped someone else understand what I was actually promising.

Consider this scenario. Joe, a colleague in operations, builds an AI assistant that answers questions about internal procedures. He tests it against a small collection of documents. His colleagues find the answers useful and want to use it. Their manager suggests launching across the department next month. IT agrees to assess how it would connect to the company’s knowledge base.

By the next executive meeting, the update reads: “Assistant complete. Awaiting IT integration.”

A demonstration has become a launch commitment. IT’s offer to investigate has become the remaining task.

Clarify the promise before the date travels

Before explaining what Joe’s assistant still needs, I would ask what his prototype reveals about us.

He understood a recurring frustration: colleagues spending time searching for procedures or asking someone who knew where to look. He produced something they found useful. If that improvement would have spent months in our backlog, we should examine why.

Did we underestimate the problem? Was our intake process too demanding for the size of the request? Did watching colleagues use the assistant reveal something a requirements document had missed?

The prototype gives us evidence worth investigating. We can see which questions people ask, which documents help them and where the existing knowledge base makes answers difficult to find.

That first conversation matters. If we respond mainly with requirements Joe has not met, colleagues may learn that involving IT makes their work harder. They may bring us the next application even later.

Before asking why IT is holding up the launch, I would ask what everyone heard when we agreed to help.

Joe thinks he has demonstrated a promising solution. IT has agreed to assess a connection. The manager expects a launch.

Everyone can leave the same meeting encouraged without recognizing that they have understood it differently.

Our language helps that misunderstanding take hold. “We’ll take a look” leaves the next step undefined. “We should be able to support this” may sound like confirmation that the proposed date is achievable.

Correcting the interpretation gets harder once the date has been shared. Asking questions then can look like retreating from a promise others believe we made.

The discomfort deserves attention. Are we leaving an assumption unchallenged because we want to appear responsive? Are we worried that clarifying the work will sound like resistance?

Before the date travels further, I would say plainly: “We have agreed to assess the connection. We have not yet confirmed the work or the launch date.”

Explain the work behind the launch

During the assessment, IT discovers that Joe manually selected the documents used in the demonstration. The wider knowledge base contains older versions of procedures and documents with different access restrictions. The prototype has not been tested against conflicting sources or questions the documents cannot answer.

Nobody has agreed who will maintain the source material or investigate an incorrect response after launch.

IT needs to make that remaining work understandable. “Security review pending” tells the sponsor where the assistant is sitting, but little about what needs to happen.

A more useful explanation is: “The wider knowledge base includes documents with different access permissions. We need to verify that employees cannot receive information through the assistant that they are not authorized to access in the source documents.”

Then explain who owns that work, what happens next and when the sponsor can expect an estimate. If a decision is needed, name it.

I would hold IT accountable for those answers. A team that identifies concerns without providing a route forward can become the bottleneck colleagues describe. Better wording will not fix an indefinite review queue.

We also need to justify the level of scrutiny. A limited trial using approved, nonsensitive documents may warrant a lighter assessment than an assistant searching restricted information or advising employees on consequential decisions.

Microsoft’s guidance for Copilot Studio distinguishes personal experimentation, departmental use and mission-critical enterprise applications, with governance controls suited to each. I would use that distinction to discuss what the proposed launch actually involves.

Agree on the next commitment

Gartner’s 2026 survey found that only 31% of CIOs reported having guidelines for deciding when an AI pilot should not advance to production. At the first discussion about wider adoption, I would ask three questions to establish what we are ready to promise.

1. What has the prototype demonstrated?

Give the sponsor an accurate account to share: “Joe has shown that an assistant can help colleagues find answers in a selected collection of procedures. We have not yet assessed it against the wider knowledge base, different access permissions or conflicting sources.”

2. What must be true for the next intended use?

I would first agree on the next step. A supervised trial with five users and approved documents is a different commitment from departmental access to the wider knowledge base.

For that step, identify the essential conditions, who will meet them and how readiness will be judged. Agree on representative questions, expected answers and what the assistant should do when it cannot find sufficient information. NIST’s Generative AI Profile identifies pre-deployment testing as a central consideration in managing generative AI risks. I would ask the team to show what its tests establish about this intended use.

Name the business owner responsible for the source material alongside the technical owners responsible for access, integration and support.

Keep Joe involved where his knowledge helps. His initiative should not automatically make him responsible for maintaining the assistant indefinitely.

3. What would we need to change to commit to it?

Establish whether the work fits within available capacity. If it does, say so. If it competes with existing commitments, identify which ones and involve the affected owners.

“Capacity is tight” gives the sponsor little to act on. “This needs the integration team assigned to the migration” makes the choice visible. Explain the consequence and recommend a workable option.

Include the business work too. Reviewing procedures and resolving conflicting documents require time from people outside IT. A launch plan that assumes their availability without agreement is incomplete.

Before the meeting ends, ask the sponsor to describe what they will report to the executive team. If they say “launch next month” while your team believes it has agreed to an assessment, the misunderstanding is already present.

Resolve it there. Once the date enters the executive update, clarifying the commitment may look like changing it.

If Joe’s assistant needs the integration team assigned to a platform migration, I would bring a recommendation to the discussion.

I would assess whether to revise a migration milestone, obtain qualified capacity or narrow the initial deployment. A trial limited to approved documents could help the team evaluate usefulness while the broader connection is assessed.

Explain the consequences, identify what remains uncertain and state which option you support.

We also owe Joe’s idea a fair comparison with work already approved. His prototype may reveal a better use of resources. Are we protecting the migration because its next milestone matters more or because it is already in our plan?

The next executive update is a test of whether that discussion worked.

“Assistant complete. Awaiting IT integration” conceals the decisions still needed. A useful update might say:

“Joe’s prototype helped colleagues find answers in selected procedures. We have approved a five-user trial using a reviewed document set. Broader launch remains subject to permissions testing, content ownership and a decision about integration capacity.”

Sometimes IT really is taking too long. We owe colleagues a proportionate assessment, a recommendation and a credible next step.

We also owe our teams clarity about what we have promised. Before the next demonstration becomes a launch announcement, ask the sponsor what they believe has been agreed.

Then ask yourself: did my offer to help sound like a promise to deliver?

item.title: One Identity Unveils Active Roles 8.6 with Enhanced Security and Administration
item.description:
Active Roles 8.6: Cumulative security, feature and administration upgrades 

One Identity has introduced Active Roles 8.6, strengthening secure and streamlined Active Directory administration with cumulative platform improvements, expanded API capabilities and greater authentication flexibility.

Active Roles 8.6, updated July 27, 2026, focuses on security and cumulative platform improvements. It fixes an RSTS configuration security issue and supersedes versions 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5. Compared with Active Roles 8.2.1 SP6, One Identity says 8.6 incorporates the features, enhancements and resolved issues delivered across that intervening release line. See the Active Roles 8.6 Release Notes.

The recent improvements are therefore best described as an administrator and integration experience upgrade, rather than a new visual redesign. The cumulative release line adds capabilities including the Active Roles REST API, as well as Redistributable Secure Token Server capabilities supporting API access and SAML 2.0 federated authentication. 

Active Roles 8.6: Familiar Administration Meets Greater Flexibility and Consolidation 

Those upgrades complement one of Active Roles’ most recognizable usability strengths: a flexible, configurable UI that can be tailored to individual users and personas. Its thick-client interface is designed to resemble the familiar Microsoft Active Directory experience, helping reduce the learning curve for experienced AD administrators. 

The broader experience centers on consolidation, with a single console spanning Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 helping administrators avoid constantly switching between separate management environments. Together with PowerShell and VBScript support, the product keeps familiar tools and interaction patterns at the center of the administrator experience. 

This combination of configurable views, familiar administration and centralized control supports Active Roles’ position among top Active Directory management solutions. 

#1 Peerspot Position Strengthens the Ease-of-Administration Story 

PeerSpot currently ranks Active Roles by One Identity #1 in Active Directory Management, with an 8.5/10 rating based on 92 reviews. It also reports the largest category mindshare at 11.7%, up from 10.4% year over year, and identifies Active Roles as the category’s most popular solution by searches. [peerspot.com] 

The PeerSpot assessment highlights automated user provisioning, lifecycle management, role-based access control, password resets and streamlined account management among capabilities that reduce manual effort. 

Feature in focus: Administrator experience with Active Roles 8.6 

Active Roles 8.6 is an administrator-experience evolution, combining cumulative security, API and authentication improvements with the product’s established configurable UI, familiar Microsoft-style experience and consolidated hybrid administration.
